newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak party says banking row may bring early poll.
newsitem.headline: Slovak party says banking row may bring early poll.

text.p: A junior member of Slovakia's ruling coalition, the Slovak National Party (SNS), said on Friday that a row within the government over banking privatisation may lead to early elections.

The same issue caused a crisis last year in Slovakia's coalition government but has now resurfaced because the opposition and a left-wing party in the government want bank privatisation to be halted at least until the end of 2003.

"If some political power able to settle the situation doesn't appear soon, the development will probably lead to early elections," Jaroslav Paska, an SNS member of parliament and former Minister of Education, told a news conference.
While Paska said the SNS would do nothing to disrupt the coalition, Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar has said he may tie the issue to a vote of confidence in his government.
Parliamentary elections are due by autumn next year.
Paska cited the row inside the ruling coalition over the privatisation of the country's banking sector as a major problem pulling the three-party government apart.
Last Thursday, parliament approved a measure halting banking privatisation until the end of 2003 at the earliest.

The SNS and Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS) both opposed the law. But all 12 deputies of another minor coalition member, the ultra-left Workers' Party (ZRS), joined the opposition and helped push through the legislation.
The government said on Tuesday it was planning to reject the law, which has to be signed by both the president and prime minister before it can take effect.
Meciar said he was considering linking a new vote on bank privatisation with a confidence vote for his cabinet.
"As far as I know, it has not yet been officially decided to link these two (votes) together, but if it happens, the SNS will support the government," Paska said.
"The privatisation of banks is an important part of the entire economic transformation in Slovakia, therefore I would find it justified if it was linked with the confidence vote," he added.

The state-controlled National Property Fund (NPF) controls 91.3 percent of the largest savings bank Slovenska Sporitelna, 50.5 percent in the insurance company Slovenska Poistovna, some 35 percent in bank IRB and about 17 percent in the largest commercial bank VUB.

The problem for Meciar is that, under the Slovak constitution, a law rejected by the prime minister and president can still get final ratification if it is sent back to parliament -- providing it then wins the backing of a simple majority of the deputies.
Opposition parties and the ZRS say they will again vote to postpone bank privatisation if the law is returned to parliament.
The leader of the ZRS, Jan Luptak, said his party would stick to that line even if it meant destroying the government.

"We will vote for this law again, regardless of any possible conditions linked to it," Luptak said on Thursday. "We would not destroy the coalition; it would be destroyed only by those who will link the law with the confidence vote."

Last June's row over the issue was eventually settled within Meciar's coalition and parliament later approved a law stopping bank privatisation until March 31, 1997. With that deadline about to expire, a new decision is needed.
